related_questions.question: How does Connecticut calculate child support?

text_blocks.snippet: In Connecticut, child support is primarily calculated using the "income shares" model, which aims to ensure children receive the same financial support they would have if their parents lived together. This involves determining each parent's net weekly income, combining them, and then applying the state's child support guidelines. The guidelines specify a base support obligation based on the number of children and the combined net income. For parents with higher combined incomes (above $4,000 per week), the court has some discretion in setting the support amount.

list.title: Income Determination:
list.snippet: The process starts with calculating each parent's gross income, then deducting allowable expenses like taxes, health insurance, and mandatory retirement contributions to arrive at net income.

list.title: Income Shares Model:
list.snippet: The core principle is that children are entitled to the same financial support they would receive if their parents lived together. The combined net income of both parents is used to determine a base support obligation.

list.title: Child Support Guidelines:
list.snippet: Connecticut has established child support guidelines that outline the support obligation based on the combined net weekly income of the parents and the number of children.

list.title: Deviation from Guidelines:
list.snippet: While the guidelines are a starting point, the court can deviate from them in certain situations, such as when a parent has significant assets, there's a large income disparity between parents, or the child has significant needs.

list.title: Factors Considered:
list.snippet: The court may also consider other factors like the age, health, and educational needs of the child, as well as the parents' vocational skills, earning capacity, and financial resources.

list.title: Online Calculators:
list.snippet: While online child support calculators are available, it's important to be aware that they may not always reflect the most up-to-date guidelines, and the court may order a different amount in your specific case, according to legal resources.

list.title: Legal Advice:
list.snippet: Consulting with an experienced family law attorney is recommended to understand how the guidelines apply to your specific situation, says a family law firm.

related_questions.question: Do you have to pay child support if you have 50/50 custody in Connecticut?
related_questions.snippet: The Connecticut theory is that a child should receive the same proportion of parental income as he or she would have received if the parents lived together. In other words, even when parents have joint custody, there may be child support moving from the higher-earning parent to the lower-earning parent.

related_questions.snippet: Retroactive child support, also known as back child support, may be issued if a noncustodial parent owed support during a particular time period and had the money to pay it. There is no statute of limitations on child support in the state of Connecticut, meaning that a parent can file for child support at any time.
